companies.market: ASML sells lithography machines, the tools that print a chip's circuit pattern with light onto a wafer (a thin silicon disc later cut into chips), plus the service, upgrades and software that keep them running. Its most advanced line uses extreme ultraviolet light (EUV, light of a very short wavelength that can print the finest features). Its newest EUV design, High-NA (optics that gather more light, to print still finer features), has gone mostly to customers' research sites, and the filing says ASML has now released its first full-specification High-NA machine to its first customer. The filing says ASML is currently the world's only maker of EUV machines, and names Canon and Nikon as rivals only in the older deep-ultraviolet machines. Its buyers are chip factories making logic (processors) and memory. In 2025 its logic sales grew, driven by foundries (factories that make chips to other firms' designs) building for AI demand, while its memory sales fell; sales of older machines in China were stronger than it expected. ASML files a 20-F (the annual report foreign companies file with the US regulator) under IFRS, the international accounting rules, so this site's filing reader records no figures for it.
must_be_true: The world keeps building factories for the newest processes (the latest generations of chip-making, which print the smallest features) in logic and memory faster than old ones retire, so demand for EUV machines grows rather than just replacing worn tools.

Chip makers keep shrinking features with lithography rather than with other processes that would need fewer of its machines; the filing names competition from alternative technologies or manufacturing processes only in general terms.
High-NA EUV reaches mass production and customers adopt it on the finest layers, so the next generation is also ASML's alone.
Zeiss and ASML's other single-source suppliers can grow output fast enough that their capacity does not cap its sales for years at a time.
Export rules between the United States, the Netherlands and China do not shut it out of a large block of buyers while a state-backed rival learns to build competing machines.

Customers design their factory processes around its machines and buy its service and upgrades for years after; its service and upgrade sales grew faster than machine sales in 2025, though the filing says part of that came from upgrades to installed EUV machines being counted there instead of as machine sales.

companies.market: Micron makes memory chips: DRAM (the working memory a processor reads and writes constantly), NAND (the storage that keeps data when power is off) and high-bandwidth memory, or HBM (DRAM dies, single chips cut from a silicon wafer, stacked and placed beside an AI chip so they can feed it data very fast). It sells to cloud firms, server makers, phone and PC makers and car makers, and reorganised in 2025 around business units, one of which serves the largest cloud buyers and holds all its HBM sales to data centres. Memory has long been a cyclical, commodity market: its 10-K (the annual report US companies file with their regulator) warns that an oversupplied market pushes prices down, and that heavy investment, including by Chinese state-backed makers, threatens oversupply. This site's filed figures show the swing: Micron made a gross loss (sales below the direct cost of making them) in 2023, and has since swung from losses to a gross margin, the share of sales kept after those costs, among the highest this site has recorded for it. How big the market becomes depends on whether AI keeps memory short, and for how long.
must_be_true: AI keeps raising the amount of memory each unit of computing needs, so memory demand grows faster than the makers can add capacity, cycle after cycle.

powers.a cornered resource: preferential access to something others need: a patent, a licence, a scarce input, a rare team
powers.branding: buyers pay more for the same thing because of what they believe about who made it
powers.counter-positioning: a newcomer's model the incumbent could copy only by damaging its own business
powers.network economies: each user makes the product more valuable to the others, so the leader's lead feeds itself
powers.process power: a way of working that improves cost or quality and takes a rival years to learn
powers.scale economies: unit costs fall as volume grows, and a rival cannot match them without matching the volume
powers.switching costs: a customer would lose money, time or work by moving to a rival

units.case: NVIDIA and AMD take [fact:chips_gp_share] of the gross profit (sales minus the direct cost of making them) that this site can measure across chips, one cloud and the leading labs; that share is up on the year, though it slipped in the latest quarter. Yet chips from other designers already make up [fact:silicon_share_now] of the AI computing shipped so far, including custom chips that Broadcom and others build for large cloud and model companies. TSMC's filing calls its scale and capacity, particularly for advanced processes (the newest generations of chip-making, which print the smallest features), a major competitive advantage, and its biggest customers as a group have taken a larger part of its revenue each year since 2023, even as its single largest customer's share fell. ASML says it is currently the world's only maker of extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines, which print the finest features with light of a very short wavelength, and that one supplier, Carl Zeiss, makes all their optics and limits how many it can build. Against this unit, this site reads foundry supply as easing: TSMC's capacity is catching up with demand. That undercuts the title's claim for the foundry only if the easing reaches TSMC's own prices and margins, which this site cannot yet see, since TSMC files under international accounting rules this site's filing reader does not read. The three designers' own conditions do not collide: NVIDIA's, Broadcom's and AMD's can all hold at once until chips from other designers make up most of the AI computing shipped.
units.commoditising: Chips made on older processes are cheap and interchangeable; TSMC's own filing says rivals in those processes are numerous. This site judges that the cost of a unit of computing keeps falling with each chip generation, and that the general-purpose AI chip is being copied from below: every large buyer that designs its own chip, often with Broadcom's help, turns part of NVIDIA's market into a price to negotiate. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers as lower prices and better products.
units.converts_if: For the designer: its software (for NVIDIA, CUDA, the platform developers write AI code against) and its whole-rack systems with their own links between chips keep buyers even when rival chips are plentiful and cheaper, turning a shortage rent into switching costs, what a customer would lose by moving to a rival. For the foundry and the toolmaker: they keep a lead at each new process, so their scale and process power outlive the AI shortage.
units.kill_shot: NVIDIA keeping both its share of AI chip supply and its gross margin while AMD's chips and the custom chips ship in volume and wafer supply at the newest processes keeps growing fast; or a second foundry making AI chips at the newest process in volume for a major designer.
units.mechanism: Three kinds of firm make AI chips. Designers such as NVIDIA, AMD and Broadcom draw them; a foundry (a factory that makes chips to other firms' designs), above all TSMC, prints them onto wafers (thin discs of silicon, each later cut into many chips); and toolmakers such as ASML build the machines that do the printing. Eliyahu Goldratt, a physicist who studied factories, found that a system runs at the pace of its slowest part. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. So while buyers cannot get enough chips, the designer they most want takes the rent. This site judges that as more chips arrive and the biggest buyers design their own, that rent is exposed, while the foundry and the toolmaker keep theirs for as long as no rival can match what they do.

rival.title: Some link in the chip chain proves easier to expand

units.stays_scarce: This site judges that capacity at the newest processes, and the machines that print it, stay scarce. A new factory for the newest process takes years to build and the skill to run it takes longer. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier, and named the kinds that recur. Two apply here: process power (a way of working that takes rivals years to learn) and scale economies (unit costs that fall as volume grows, so a rival must match the volume to match the cost). The EUV machines have one maker, fed by one optics supplier: a cornered resource, Helmer's term for preferential access to something others need, which does not ease when chips do.

units.case: SK hynix reported record results for 2025, with HBM revenue growing sharply and demand for ordinary server memory rising sharply too. Samsung describes low inventory and supply constraints in memory. This site's tightness word for memory reads moderate, though memory is counted in dollars, so a price rise looks like more memory. Micron's own filing warns that if HBM demand weakens and makers shift capacity back to ordinary DRAM, its supply could rise sharply, and that an oversupplied market pushes prices down; it also names Chinese state-backed makers, CXMT and YMTC, among the causes of that risk.
units.commoditising: Ordinary memory, the kind in phones and laptops, is a textbook commodity: identical parts, several makers, and prices that swing with each wave of new factories. Networking built to open standards such as Ethernet, which Broadcom sells to the largest cloud and model companies, is interchangeable by design. Eliyahu Goldratt, a physicist who studied factories, found that a system runs at the pace of its slowest part, and David Ricardo, an English economist who studied why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. On their account the rent in memory lasts only until the makers build their way out, and SK hynix says it is building new factories in Korea.
units.converts_if: Custom HBM, memory built to one buyer's design, which SK hynix calls a key differentiator, becomes the norm, so each chip generation is locked to one maker and switching costs replace the shortage. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than rivals, named switching costs, what a customer would lose by moving to a rival, as one of the lasting advantages he found. In networking, the rent lasts only if NVIDIA's own links stay faster than open standards by enough that buyers accept being tied to one vendor.

units.mechanism: An AI chip is only as fast as the memory that feeds it. High-bandwidth memory, or HBM, is DRAM (the working memory a processor reads and writes constantly) cut into dies (single chips), stacked and placed beside the processor so data reaches it quickly. This site counts three makers: SK hynix, Samsung and Micron. Micron's filing says HBM needs more wafers (the silicon discs chips are cut from) and more factory space than ordinary DRAM for the same amount of memory, so when AI demand runs ahead the makers profit, and if it weakens they can turn the same factories back to ordinary memory. Networking, the switches, cables and light-based links that join many chips into one machine, splits in two: NVIDIA's own links, which tie buyers to its systems, and gear built to open standards, which any maker can supply.

Against this unit, power generated on site beside the data centre, and chips that do more work for each unit of electricity, would both loosen the grid's hold. David Teece, an economist who studied why the firm that invents something often fails to keep the returns, called the inputs an innovation needs to reach its customers complementary assets; generic ones, which anyone can buy, earn an ordinary return, not a rent.

This site judges that buildings and money can be had quickly, while a new connection means waiting for the utility to add lines and transformers, and new power stations take years. Eliyahu Goldratt, a physicist who studied factories, found that a system runs at the pace of its slowest part; David Ricardo, an English economist who studied why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. So, in this site's judgement, the rent goes to whoever already holds land with power and a connection. Much of that input sits with utilities whose prices a regulator sets, so they cannot charge what the shortage is worth; this site judges that the rent leaks instead to owners of connected sites and of power stations already running.

A connection is close to a licence: a utility grants it under a regulator's rules and it cannot be copied, which makes it what Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied lasting advantages, calls a cornered resource: preferential access to something others need. Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, and Oliver Williamson, who studied contracts and found that a buyer who depends on an asset built for it can be squeezed by whoever owns it, would expect the largest buyers to own such assets or lock them up in long contracts.

units.case: The big clouds' own segment profits are high: this site's filed figures show AWS, Google Cloud and Microsoft's cloud segment each earning a high operating margin (profit after running costs, as a share of sales), one that moves up and down from quarter to quarter. Oracle's filing says some of its cloud offerings are concentrated among a number of large customers, and that some customers may be heavily in debt. Their spending runs far ahead of AI's revenue: the biggest cloud and platform companies spend [fact:capex_to_revenue] as much a year on buildings and equipment as AI earns in revenue. Microsoft's remaining performance obligations (revenue customers have signed for but not yet received) stand at [fact:msft_backlog] its revenue over the past year, against [fact:msft_backlog_year_ago] a year before. The clouds also fund their own customers: Microsoft's filing calls it a major investor in OpenAI with rights to OpenAI's models, and Amazon's filing records investments in Anthropic and a large gain on them in 2025. The hourly rent for NVIDIA's previous-generation flagship chip changed by [fact:h100_rent_yoy] over the past year on this site's latest reading (a minus sign would mark a fall).
units.commoditising: This site judges that an hour on a given GPU is becoming a commodity: the same NVIDIA chips are rented by many firms, Nebius names CoreWeave, Crusoe and Lambda as well as the big clouds among its rivals, and CoreWeave says its customers specify NVIDIA's chips, so the chip, not the cloud, is what they are buying. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers as lower prices. On that finding, the rent on each generation of chips falls towards cost as those chips become plentiful. David Teece, an economist who studied why the firm that invents something often fails to keep the returns, called the inputs a product needs to reach its customers complementary assets. This site judges that a neocloud's rack of rented chips is a generic one, which anyone with money, power and a supply of chips can assemble; the scarce inputs behind it belong to others, NVIDIA's chips on one side and the demand of a few big buyers on the other.
units.converts_if: The big clouds turn chip rental into services customers build on, such as their own chips, their own model catalogues and the tools that run AI inside a firm's data, so switching costs hold AI work as they hold older work. For a neocloud: long take-or-pay contracts with buyers who can pay, signed during the shortage, outlast it, and it wins powered sites others cannot get, a cornered resource in Helmer's term (preferential access to something others need). Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, and Oliver Williamson, who found that a buyer that depends on an asset built for it can be squeezed by its owner, would expect the biggest buyers to build their own capacity once they can, which is the risk a neocloud's contracts must outlast.
units.kill_shot: Big-cloud margins falling to the neoclouds' level as AI becomes most of what they sell, with customers moving AI work between clouds on price alone; or a neocloud keeping its margin through a year in which GPU rents fall steeply and its largest customer leaves at the end of its contract.
units.mechanism: A cloud rents out computing by the hour or by the contract. The big clouds, often called hyperscalers (Microsoft's Azure, Amazon's AWS, Google Cloud and Oracle), sell AI chips alongside storage, databases and the software businesses already run on them. The neoclouds (newer firms such as CoreWeave, Nebius, Crusoe, Lambda and Fluidstack that rent out mostly NVIDIA's graphics chips, GPUs, and little else) sell the chips almost alone. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. This site judges that a neocloud's margin is that kind of rent, the gap between what a scarce chip rents for and what it costs to buy, power and borrow against, and that it lasts while chips and powered buildings are short; a big cloud's margin rests more on customers whose data and systems already sit inside it.

units.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is powered, connected data-centre space and, for the big clouds, the customer relationships and the data already stored with them. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier. Scale economies and switching costs apply to the big clouds' existing business today: scale economies (unit costs that fall as volume grows, so a rival must match the volume to match the cost; Google offers its own AI chips, TPUs, beside GPUs) and switching costs (what a customer would lose by moving to a rival, here the work of moving data and systems built around one cloud). units.case: Open models trail the best closed ones by [fact:open_lag] on this site's latest reading, and on OpenRouter, a service that routes developers' requests to many models, open models took [fact:open_share] of the tokens among its most used models. The price of a given level of capability falls steeply on the estimate of Epoch, a research group that tracks AI, which this site reads as emerging. Against that, the businesses paying for AI, on the card and bill-payment data of Ramp, a firm that handles companies' spending, are concentrated among few labs, while the developers routing through OpenRouter spread their tokens across many more labs. The labs spend far ahead of their revenue: for OpenAI and Anthropic, a year of revenue at the current pace is well below the equity (money investors paid for shares) each has raised, and this site's last reading for xAI, taken before its merger into SpaceX, was also well below. Those revenue figures come mostly from the labs themselves, and investors value the labs at many times that revenue. The labs are buying their way up the stack, into the layers above them that sit closer to users: this site's acquisition ledger counts [fact:lab_deals_now] deals in the past year by which model and computing firms took companies in the layers above, including OpenAI's purchases of consumer apps and of a firm that installs AI inside companies, and Anthropic's of developer tools. Some labs already reach users directly: Google puts its Gemini model into Search and its apps, OpenAI reaches consumers through ChatGPT, its chat app, and Microsoft, which is not a frontier lab on this site's map, holds rights to OpenAI's models for its own products and has a revenue-share agreement with OpenAI. The strongest case against this site's judgement comes from Giovanni Cattani, an investor at Hummingbird Ventures, a venture capital firm, and before that an analyst at Blackstone, a private-investment firm. In an article he published on X, the social network, in early September 2026, titled 'Nobody is talking seriously about AI demand', he argued that the frontier labs' revenue rests on a few open-ended, long tasks, such as AI research, writing software and trading, where buyers always want the best model and will pay the labs' margins; on work with a natural limit, he argued, cheaper models from outside the frontier, firms that run models for others, and small models tuned to one job win instead. On that view the rent holds for as long as the uses of AI keep spreading into open-ended work.
units.commoditising: This site judges that answering a well-understood request, the kind a model from a year before could already handle, is a commodity: many labs and open models do it, and it is priced close to the cost of the chips and power that run it. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers as lower prices and better products. Kenneth Arrow, an economist who studied how markets handle knowledge, argued that information is hard to own because copying it is cheap; a model's behaviour can be observed and partly copied by a rival training on its answers.
units.converts_if: Labs turn deployments into switching costs: their coding agents, business tools and staff inside customers become part of how firms work, so moving to a rival means rebuilding, not just repointing. Or a lab owns the place users meet AI, as a chat app with a habit behind it, which Helmer would call branding (a buyer pays more for the same thing because of its name) or network economies (the product grows more useful as more people use it). David Teece, an economist who studied why inventors often fail to keep the returns from what they invent, found that the firm holding the complementary assets (the distribution, sales and systems a product needs to reach buyers) often keeps the profit; Google and Meta already hold theirs, and OpenAI and Anthropic are buying theirs. The rent also lasts, without either, if open-ended uses where only the best model will do keep growing faster than bounded ones, the case Giovanni Cattani makes above. Rules could entrench it too: Sayash Kapoor and Arvind Narayanan, computer scientists at Princeton who study what AI can and cannot do, argued that licensing who may build models, combined with limits on sharing them, would leave only a handful of firms able to build the most capable ones; this site reads that as a route to a regulatory rent (a profit protected by a licence rivals cannot get), which would make the lead last.
units.kill_shot: Labs keeping their price premium and their share of business spending on models that open ones already match, with no growth in deployments or products; or, the other way, business spending spreading across many labs and open models as freely as developers' routed tokens already do.
units.mechanism: The frontier labs, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, xAI and Meta, train the most capable AI models: programs trained on huge amounts of text and data to write, reason and carry out tasks. They sell their use by the token (a fragment of a word) and through products such as chat apps and coding tools. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. Today the scarce input is the best model, and the lab that has it charges for it. This site judges that the rent on a lead is transitional, because open-weight models (whose trained settings, the weights, are published for anyone to run) arrive some months behind, and that it becomes durable only where a lab is woven into how its customers work or owns the place where users meet it.

rival.title: The labs are durable businesses with high margins

units.stays_scarce: This site judges that the newest model at the frontier stays scarce for as long as it leads, and that training one costs so much in chips and money that only a handful of firms attempt it. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier; the one that clearly applies today is scale economies (the cost of training a model is fixed, so a lab with more users spreads it thinner, and a rival must match the users to match the cost). Switching costs (what a customer would lose by moving to a rival) are emerging, not proven: they exist where a lab's tools are built into a firm's systems, but this site cannot yet measure how often firms use several labs at once, so it does not count them in this group's powers.
units.title: A frontier lab's lead earns a rent that open models chase within months; it lasts only where the lab is built into its customers' work

units.case: This site has revenue readings for few of the neolabs. The voice specialist ElevenLabs reports a run-rate (a recent month's revenue scaled up to a year) that rose fast from the end of 2025 to April 2026 and more slowly since, evidence that a specialist off the big labs' path can earn money. For Mistral, a year of revenue at the current pace is well below the equity it has raised, though that gap has narrowed during 2026. The frontier labs' own costs are the hurdle: training at the frontier costs so much that, on this site's reading, even the leading labs' revenue is well below what they have raised. The specialists face a different test: open models trail the best closed ones by only [fact:open_lag], so a new lab's lead in a general model is short-lived, while a specialty in voice, video, robots or science may lie outside what the general labs train for. This site's acquisition ledger counts only purchases of firms in the layers above the models, so it cannot show a neolab being bought, or its leaders hired, by a bigger lab. This site judges which neolabs sit off the big labs' path; it does not measure it.
units.commoditising: This site judges that a general model from a new lab is commoditising fastest of all: it competes with the frontier labs above it and the open-weight labs below it. Kenneth Arrow, an economist who studied how markets handle knowledge, argued that information is hard to own because copying it is cheap; a research idea, once published or seen in a product, spreads to labs with more chips. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers.
units.converts_if: A specialist's product becomes the tool a trade works in, so switching costs (what a customer would lose by moving to a rival) hold customers after the general labs catch up; or its data from customers and experiments passes Hagiu and Wright's tests and becomes a cornered resource, Helmer's term for preferential access to something others need. A general neolab converts only if its different route (a new way to train, or a model that learns after it is released) proves both better and hard to copy.
units.kill_shot: A lab founded since 2023 taking the lead on general models and holding it while charging for it; or the specialists' niches being matched by the frontier labs' general models, with the specialists' prices falling to the general labs' level.
units.mechanism: Neolabs are younger AI labs outside the big frontier group, most founded in the last few years and mostly funded by investors before they sell much: Mistral, which publishes the weights (the trained settings) of some of its models, Safe Superintelligence, Thinking Machines Lab, Reflection AI and Periodic Labs among the general and research labs; ElevenLabs, Black Forest Labs and others in voice, images and video; Physical Intelligence and Skild AI in robots. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. For a new lab the scarce input is its researchers and its bet on a route the big labs are not taking. This site judges that where that route leads somewhere the frontier labs are heading anyway, the new lab competes with them for chips and money on worse terms, and its people are worth more to a big lab than its business is to investors.

rival.title: The lead among labs keeps changing hands

units.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is the small number of researchers who can lead a frontier training run (the training of the most capable model of its time), and in the specialties, the data and tuning for one kind of work (a voice, a robot's movements, a laboratory's experiments) that general labs have not collected. Andrei Hagiu and Julian Wright, economists who asked when learning from customers' data keeps rivals out, found it does so only when the data is proprietary, keeps its value and improves the product for every customer; a specialty that passes those tests may hold. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier; this site finds no such power proven in the neolabs today.
units.title: A new lab earns a rent only where its specialty lies off the big labs' path; elsewhere its asset is its people

units.case: These readings cover all open models, including Meta's and Mistral's, not only this group's. Open models trail the best closed ones by [fact:open_lag] on this site's latest reading, and on OpenRouter, a service that routes developers' requests to many models, they took [fact:open_share] of the tokens among its most used models, though OpenRouter's users lean towards cheap models and firms that buy from the labs directly never appear there. This site reads the open models' gap to the closed frontier on Epoch's capability index (a score from Epoch, a research group that tracks AI, combining many tests of what a model can do) as unclear: it moves both ways between readings. The labs' finances differ: for MiniMax and Zhipu, a year of revenue at the current pace now exceeds what they raised in their share listings, the only rounds this site records for them; for DeepSeek it is far below.
units.commoditising: The open model is a commodity by design: many hosts serve the same weights and compete on price, so the price of running it falls towards the cost of the chips and power. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers as lower prices and better products. This site judges open-weight labs are the clearest case of it in AI: the buyers and the hosts keep most of what the model is worth.
units.converts_if: An open-weight lab's parent earns what the lab gives away: a cloud whose customers come for the free model and stay for the services, which David Teece, an economist who studied why inventors often fail to keep the returns from what they invent, would call owning the complementary assets (the hosting, sales and systems a product needs to reach buyers). Or giving the model away becomes counter-positioning in Helmer's sense, a model a closed lab cannot copy without cutting into its own paid business, with the parent collecting the reward.
units.kill_shot: Closed labs keeping their prices on models that open ones already match, with open models' share of use falling; or an open-weight lab earning a lasting profit on the model itself rather than on hosting, services or a parent.
units.mechanism: An open-weight lab publishes its model's weights, the trained settings that are the model, so anyone can run it on their own chips or rent it from a host. This site's open-weight labs include DeepSeek, Alibaba's Qwen team, Moonshot, MiniMax, Zhipu and StepFun, all of them Chinese; Meta's Llama models are open too, though this site counts Meta among the frontier labs and Mistral among the new labs. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. A model anyone can copy is not scarce, so the lab that publishes it collects little rent on it; this site judges that it earns instead through hosting its own model, selling a better closed version, or serving a parent company or state that wants the model to exist.

rival.title: Labs charge for their lead and let buyers go

units.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is the skill to train a model near the frontier on fewer chips, which some of these labs have shown, and the chips themselves, which export rules make harder for Chinese labs to buy. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier; this site finds none proven for the open-weight labs, because a skill that shows up in a published model can be studied and copied.
units.title: Open-weight labs give the model away, so they keep little of its value but cap what the closed labs can charge
